transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marco Li (Redwood Platform Eng), Dana Ortiz (Redwood Solutions), Tom Hargreaves (Lumen Lead ML Eng), Sofia Ramos (Lumen SRE), Leena Kapoor (Lumen Head of Platform), Victor Ng (Lumen Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focusing on KV cache architecture and emergent behaviors observed by Lumen in a long-context rewrite/assistant product. Topics: context sweep/hotset hysteresis, spill-to-disk vs paging, prefix reuse collisions, tenant affinity and routed batching, and operational telemetry for on-prem VPC deployment.

Topics covered:
- Hot-prefix detection windows and hysteresis thresholds
- Eviction/trimming heuristics under bursty long-context loads
- Spill/paging strategies: async spill, read-ahead (read ahead) and eviction quotas
- Prefix reuse heuristics and tenant affinity reroute
- Interaction between quantized kernels and KV cache eviction timings
- Security/operational concerns for on-prem NVMe spill and KMS integration

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Okay, hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna jump straight into the context sweep notes from the logs you shared, Tom. Priya and Marco are gonna walk through hypotheses and some mitigations.
[00:12] Tom (Lumen): Thanks Alex. Um, just to set context — this has been a recurring customer-reported problem where the assistant degrades after a sustained 5-10 minute conversation with multi-turn persona state. We're seeing a step function in latency around the 1500-2000 token mark, then some requests stall while systems do a "context sweep".
[00:30] Priya (Redwood): Right, that sweep wording is helpful. What we mean by sweep in our runtime is the KV reconcile/eviction pass that runs when hotset memory pressure crosses the hysteresis threshold. The key here is that the eviction pass does two things: it evicts cold prefixes and attempts to compact KV entries. If spill-to-disk is enabled, it will also trigger async spill tasks which can backpressure IO.
[00:50] Sofia (Lumen): Yeah, we suspect our long-running sessions are creating large prefix chains and the runtime spends a noticeable chunk of time doing prefix reclamation. Would that map to the reconcile you described?
[00:59] Priya (Redwood): Exactly. Reconcile is a soft-eviction sweep plus consistency trimming. By default there's an LRU-ish component and a hotscore decay that tries to avoid thrashing. But with highly correlated prefixes — think: repeated user prompts that vary only in a few tokens — the hotscore can incorrectly treat new prefixes as cold because they're not exact matches.
[01:20] Leena (Lumen): So that explains the "mis-hit" behavior. Is there a way to tune the prefix matching to be more approximate or to use prefix hashing with locality?
[01:28] Marco (Redwood): We have a few levers. One is prefix coalescing: when two prefixes share a large overlap we can map them to the same hotset bucket for a short window. Another is increasing hysteresis so that you avoid frequent sweeps; the tradeoff is memory usage. We can also use a small bloom-filter style cache to keep recent variants hot.
[01:45] Victor (Lumen): Question on security: if we coalesce prefixes across tenants, do we risk cross-tenant leakage?
[01:50] Dana (Redwood): Good point. Any coalescing we do is tenant-aware; we never materialize prefix equality across tenants in the same hotset unless the customer requests multi-tenant pooling. For Lumen's private deployment we'll default to tenant isolation.
[02:02] Tom (Lumen): You mentioned async spill. Our infra team noticed NVMe saturation during the sweep windows. Can you summarize how async spill interacts with the main inference loop?
[02:12] Priya (Redwood): Sure — async spill runs in worker threads. The inference loop will mark pages for spill and return; however, if the write queue length grows past a threshold we take a backpressure signal that slows new allocations. That backpressure is intended to preserve the in-memory working set, but in your case the sustained long contexts fill the queue faster than it's drained because the RAID0-like NVMe farm is shared and experiences IOPS contention from other processes.
[02:36] Sofia (Lumen): So it's not just raw disk bandwidth; it's queueing and IO latency variability. We saw 5–20ms spikes that line up with the stalls.
[02:45] Priya (Redwood): Exactly. We recommend either increasing the write concurrency for spills (if the disk can handle it) or enabling read-ahead windows so that the runtime prefetches adjacent KV pages before the sweep completes, reducing blocking on critical requests. But read-ahead increases IO volume.
[03:00] Tom (Lumen): Is there a smart read-ahead policy? We don't want to just prefetch everything.
[03:05] Marco (Redwood): We implement an adaptive window: when we detect sequential access patterns for a given prefix series, the read-ahead scales up; with random access it shrinks. For Lumen's workload, initial traces show a lot of temporal locality — so small controlled read-ahead looks promising.
[03:18] [00:03:18] Speaker 3 (unlabeled): (murmur) we also saw some chunking in the quantized kernels...
[03:24] Priya (Redwood): I wanted to call out quantization interaction. Lower-bit kernels reduce memory per token but sometimes increase per-token compute variance. That variance can lead to uneven KV cache pressure because some requests allocate more ephemeral KV structures. In practice we suggest pairing quantization profile changes with adjusted eviction thresholds and ramping tests.
[03:45] Leena (Lumen): Can you describe a recommended ramping test?
[03:49] Priya (Redwood): Start with a single dedicated shard in your dedicated pool running the quantized model plus the adjusted eviction params. Run a 24–48 hour synthetic workload that matches your P95 conversation length and includes prefix mutation. Monitor hotset hit rates, write queue latency, and time spent in reconcile. If any reconcile passes exceed X% of CPU time (we usually set X=8%), fail the test and roll back.
[04:12] Tom (Lumen): In our telemetry, reconcile CPU jumps to 12% during incidents.
[04:17] Marco (Redwood): That's consistent with working set oscillation. Another mitigation is small-window checkpointing: periodically persist compacted segments off the primary hotset and free memory proactively during natural low-load windows.
[04:30] Sofia (Lumen): You mentioned tenant affinity and routed batching earlier — how would that help?
[04:36] Priya (Redwood): If you route requests by tenant-affinity then batches are more likely to touch similar prefixes, increasing KV reuse within the GPU's KV cache and reducing cross-tenant prefix churn. For multi-tenant bursts, routed batching reduces eviction noise. The tradeoff is slightly less optimal batch packing if traffic is low diversity.
[04:54] Victor (Lumen): Does routed batching require sticky sessions? We have autoscaling nodes and sometimes requests land on different hosts.
[05:00] Marco (Redwood): No sticky session required. The routing happens at the fronting layer — it's a policy that maps requests from the same tenant into the same serving pool for short windows (seconds). That pool maintains the hotset affinity. It's stateless in terms of session cookies.
[05:13] Alex (Redwood): Quick interjection — we should also surface the notion of "eviction signature" in your telemetry. That is, which prefix caused the reclaim to run and what prefixes were admitted vs evicted. Tom, your team logs show coarse evictions. We need to get fine-grained signatures.
[05:29] Tom (Lumen): Yes, we can add that. It'll increase log volume but it's worth it.
[05:34] [00:05:34] Speaker 2 (unlabeled): (overlap) also, sometimes the tokenizer splits cause near-duplicates so prefix matching misses...
[05:42] Priya (Redwood): Good call. Tokenizer normalization matters. We recommend canonicalizing whitespace and lowercasing certain stable tokens before prefix hashing for hotset keys — only within the hotset keyspace; do not alter the actual model input. That reduces false negatives on near-duplicate prefixes.
[05:58] Leena (Lumen): On the governance side Victor is thinking about encryption for spill-to-disk. Are spills encrypted at rest and integrated with our KMS?
[06:06] Victor (Lumen): We need to ensure HSM-backed keys for any persisted KV pages in the VPC.
[06:10] Dana (Redwood): For Redwood Private we offer optional per-customer envelope encryption for spill files and we can integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault). The spill driver can either write encrypted blobs or rely on the underlying FS encryption. We also produce audit logs for spill lifecycle events.
[06:26] Victor (Lumen): Great. Also, can we get assurance that during reconcile no unencrypted data gets swapped to a temporary path?
[06:31] Marco (Redwood): Affirmative. Our spill pipeline writes directly to the customer-designated mount point with atomic rename semantics; temporary buffers are in memory only. We can share an architecture diagram.
[06:41] Tom (Lumen): Circling back — you mentioned hotset hysteresis tuning. What's a reasonable starting point?
[06:46] Priya (Redwood): For workloads like yours we often start with a high-water mark (HWM) at 78% of hotset capacity and low-water mark (LWM) at 55%. That gives a 23% hysteresis window. If we see repeated sweeps we widen it (e.g., HWM 82 / LWM 45) but watch memory headroom.
[07:02] Sofia (Lumen): Those numbers are useful.
[07:04] [00:07:04] Speaker 4 (background): (typing)
[07:06] Alex (Redwood): Another operational trick is to set a per-tenant eviction cap during global pressure — we cap the number of prefixes evicted per tenant per reconcile to reduce noisy neighbors.
[07:18] Leena (Lumen): And if a tenant exceeds that cap, we fall back to routing them to a separate capacity pool?
[07:24] Marco (Redwood): Exactly. We offered a "burst overflow" pool concept — when an account's eviction rate is too high we reroute new requests to a dedicated burst pool with extra memory but higher cost. It's the same model variant, just different QoS.
[07:37] Tom (Lumen): That's appealing. We'll need billing visibility for burst pool usage.
[07:41] Alex (Redwood): We'll include cost telemetry per-pool in the dashboard.
[07:46] Priya (Redwood): I want to highlight a subtle bug we sometimes see with prefix reuse: when a prefix A is evicted and a new prefix B that is semantically similar is allocated shortly after, the runtime can allocate a new slot that collides with freed metadata causing brief corruption in the prefetch index. It's rare but shows up with extreme churn and short TTLs. We have a fix in our next patch that does a delayed free for metadata objects used in prefetch indices.
[08:14] Tom (Lumen): Could that cause incorrect completions or hallucinations?
[08:18] Priya (Redwood): In practice it manifests as a transient miss/higher latency, not hallucination. The model input is unchanged; it's an indexing error in the cache layer that leads to a miss where a hit should've been.
[08:29] Leena (Lumen): You mentioned delayed free — what's the memory overhead for that?
[08:33] Marco (Redwood): Minimal, typically a few percent of hotset memory during the grace window. We tune the grace window based on observed churn.
[08:44] [00:08:44] Speaker 1 (someone): (laughter)
[08:47] Priya (Redwood): We also proposed an experiment: enable a short-lived "speculative pin" for prefixes that are frequently reallocated — that pins metadata for N seconds even after eviction, essentially a tiny soft-cache to catch reuse patterns.
[08:59] Tom (Lumen): That sounds promising.
[09:02] Priya (Redwood): Operationally we'd expose it as "speculative_pin_secs" and a max-pin count.
[09:07] Victor (Lumen): Does that increase attack surface? Could a tenant pin everything to starve others?
[09:11] Dana (Redwood): We guard speculative pinning with per-tenant quotas and it's disabled by default. It's a local optimization only.
[09:18] Leena (Lumen): Switching topics — batching and routed batching: do you have suggestions to keep latency SLO while improving KV hit rates?
[09:25] Marco (Redwood): Yes — one is micro-batching with latency targets. Instead of waiting to fill a large batch we have a latency cap (e.g., 8ms) that flushes current partial batch; but when tenant-affinity is enabled we allow a slightly longer cap (12ms) to increase same-tenant coalescing. It improves KV locality while only marginally increasing p50.
[09:43] Tom (Lumen): Our p99 is the killer. Will that help p99?
[09:46] Priya (Redwood): It helps indirectly because p99 often comes from cold misses + reconcile contention. Improving cache locality reduces those cold misses. For raw outlier spikes we also recommend integrating our fallback policy that serves smaller model variants when reconcile latency exceeds threshold, but with strict logging so you can correlate quality regression.
[10:06] Sofia (Lumen): Is there tooling to replay a p99 scenario?
[10:09] Priya (Redwood): Yes, we supply a load-replay harness and a synthetic prefix generator that replays realistic token sequences and prefix mutation rates. We can parameterize it to stress the reconcile path.
[10:18] Tom (Lumen): Great, please share.
[10:21] [00:10:21] Speaker 5 (background): (affirmative)
[10:23] Alex (Redwood): A few quick notes about metrics — you'll want to emit: hotset_hits, hotset_misses, reconcile_cpu_pct, spill_write_queue_len, spill_latency_ms_p95, speculative_pin_count, prefix_coalesce_events, tenant_eviction_rate. We'll share a Grafana dashboard template.
[10:40] Leena (Lumen): On-prem specifics — our ops team runs air-gapped racks with local NVMe and limited outbound control plane access. Any gotchas?
[10:48] Marco (Redwood): For air-gapped on-prem we recommend configuring spill to use local encrypted NVMe and set the spill concurrency conservatively. Also, ensure the control plane can accept occasional telemetry bundles through your allowed egress paths; offline troubleshooting becomes harder without those logs.
[11:01] Victor (Lumen): Can we store telemetry encrypted and ship in batches?
[11:04] Marco (Redwood): Yes, we support encrypted telemetry bundles and scheduled sync windows.
[11:08] Priya (Redwood): One last performance note — kernel selection can change memory layout. When pairing quantization profiles with atomic KV operations, some kernels increase pointer indirection which slightly slows metadata scans. We recommend testing the exact kernel build you plan to ship in staging with identical hotset configs.
[11:28] Tom (Lumen): Understood.
[11:30] Alex (Redwood): Ok, let's run through the agreed action items and timeline. Priya will package sample traces and a reduced dashboard query set. Marco will provide kernel/quantization guidance documentations and a staging image. Tom and team will run a 48-hour synthetic long-context replay and share traces. We'll reconvene after the replay. Any final questions?
[11:52] Tom (Lumen): One small question — what's the recommended TTL for session prefixes? We're currently at 600s.
[11:57] Priya (Redwood): For heavy long-context you might lower TTL to 300s and rely on speculative_pin to catch reuse, or keep 600s and widen hysteresis. Both approaches work; it's a tradeoff between memory and warm-start probability. Start with lowering to 300s in a canary.
[12:12] Leena (Lumen): Thanks everyone.
[12:15] Alex (Redwood): Thanks all, we'll send the notes and proposed dashboard by end of day 2027-03-17.

Call end.

Notes about transcript quality: audio to text had a few mis-attributions and one overlapped segment around 00:03:18. Some product names spelled variably (NVMe spelled nvme, prefetch vs pre-fetch). We left those as-is to preserve natural transcription.
